title: Fast X-ray Transients as Premature-Dissipated Gamma-Ray Bursts with Magnetic-Dominated Jets
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJL
summary: Fast X-ray transients (FXTs) are extragalactic X-ray flashes with little or no accompanying $γ$-ray emission. We propose that FXTs and classical gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) share a common origin in Poynting-flux-dominated jets powered by the Blandford--Znajek mechanism. In this picture, FXTs arise when the kink instability triggers premature dissipation at small radii ($\sim 10^{11}$~cm), yielding low Lorentz factors ($Γ\lesssim 50$) and high compactness ($\ell' \gg 1$) that thermalize the emission into the soft X-ray band. When the kink criterion is not met, the jet accelerates to ultra-relativistic velocities ($Γ> 100$) and dissipates at larger radii ($\sim 10^{15}$~cm) as a standard GRB. This scenario can naturally explain the observed thermal spectra, low $E_{\rm peak}$, supernova associations, jet-break absence, and day-scale afterglow delays across five well-studied FXTs. EP240801a is explained as a boundary event, where premature dissipation does not exhaust the full magnetic energy; the residual energy is further dissipated at a typical GRB radius, producing the observed $γ$-ray prompt emission with an $\sim 80$~s time lag. A key observational prediction is that FXTs may exhibit $e^+ e^-$ annihilation line features sweeping from a few MeV to hundreds of keV within $\sim 0.01$~s.

title: Isotropic diffuse gamma-ray flux limits from Carpet-3 experiment data using neural networks with domain adaptation
summary: Diffuse gamma rays above 100 TeV probe PeV cosmic rays and astrophysical neutrino sources. Their strong attenuation on background radiation makes the observed flux sensitive to the location of the emission and to possible modifications of photon propagation. Searches for an isotropic component require rejection of an overwhelming hadronic background, but uncertainties in air-shower physics, cosmic-ray composition and detector response can lead to differences between simulated and measured events. Here we report upper limits on the isotropic diffuse gamma-ray flux from 100 TeV to 10 PeV using 1078 days of Carpet-3 observations collected between 2022 and 2026. We identify photon candidates with a neural network combining the surface-array signals and measurements from the upgraded 410 $\mathrm{m^2}$ muon detector. Unsupervised domain adaptation uses unlabeled experimental events during training to mitigate the impact of simulation--data discrepancies on the classification. The limits are among the strongest available and provide benchmarks for tests of extended Galactic emission and modified photon propagation from extragalactic sources.

title: Probing horizonless compact objects through observable signatures and images of accretion disk
summary: The observed images of M87$^*$ and Sgr A$^*$ by Event Horizon Telescope motivate us to study the spacetime geometry and accretion flow dynamics around compact objects beyond the Kerr/Schwarzschild scenario. In this work, we investigate the properties of a steady, inviscid, axisymmetric, advective accretion flow around the Zipoy-Voorhees ($γ$-metric) spacetime by solving the relativistic hydrodynamic equations. The $γ$-metric is a static, axisymmetric generalization of the Schwarzschild geometry and is characterized by a mass ($M_\bullet$) and a deformation parameter ($γ$). We examine how the deformation parameter $γ$ influences the effective potential, the location and nature of the critical points, and the resulting accretion flow topologies. Then, using relativistic thermal bremsstrahlung emissivity, we compute the spectral energy distribution and bolometric luminosity of the flow. We find that $γ$ affects the luminosity in opposite ways for the flow having outer critical point (O-type) and that having inner critical point (I-type). Finally, combining the flow properties with general relativistic ray tracing, we construct synthetic images of the accretion disk for different values of $γ$ and observer inclination angles. The resulting observed flux distribution independently confirms the trends obtained from the luminosity and spectral analyses. Although the shadow of the $γ$-metric has been shown to be consistent with the observed shadow radii of M87$^*$ and Sgr A$^*$, its accretion flow topology, the resulting radiative properties and image differ from the Schwarzschild case, thereby giving a complementary way to probe the deviations from the Schwarzschild paradigm.

title: Strongly Suppressed Cosmic-Ray Diffusion in a Wind-Blown Cavity Environment of SNR G21.8-3.0
summary: We report the discovery of a GeV $γ$-ray source spatially offset from SNR G21.8-3.0, while no significant high-energy emission is detected from the remnant itself. Using 16 yr of \emph{Fermi}-LAT observations together with $^{12}$CO ($J=1-0$) data, we show that the GeV emission is spatially associated with a localized molecular cloud located just outside a gas cavity whose boundary closely follows the SNR shell. This configuration supports a scenario in which cosmic rays (CRs) escaping from the remnant propagate through a progenitor-carved low-density cavity and illuminate nearby dense gas. Modeling of the cloud emission requires a diffusion coefficient suppressed by a factor of several tens relative to the canonical Galactic value, indicating strongly inhibited CR transport around the remnant. Rather than serving as a simple low-density escape channel, the wind-blown cavity appears to regulate CR propagation through local magnetic structure and enhanced turbulence. This system therefore provides evidence that circumstellar structures can control the escape and early transport of CRs around supernova remnants.

title: Lunar laser ranging analyses of NGLR-1 data with PEP and prospects for MPAc: towards one millimeter range precision
comment: 11 pages, 14 figures, 1 table. Comments are welcome
summary: Since 1969, Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) has provided critical data for investigating Earth-Moon dynamics, lunar internal structure, and tests of General Relativity (GR). However, the measurement precision of historical arrays (such as those from Apollo and Lunokhod missions) is inherently limited by laser pulse broadening induced by lunar librations. To overcome this limit, next-generation single Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs) of large optical diameter have been developed to eliminate pulse dispersion, enabling LLR measurements to advance from centimeter-level precision down to the millimeter scale. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of LLR observations from NGLR-1 (Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1), the first single 10cm-diameter CCR deployed on the lunar surface. Carried out using the Planetary Ephemeris Program (PEP), this study investigates individual range measurements, normal points (NPs), residuals, and observational dispersion collected by the ground stations at Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging station (APOL), Wettzell, and Grasse. The results: demonstrate the success of NGLR-1 in significantly enhancing time of flight measurement precision compared to legacy Apollo and Lunokhod retroreflector arrays; indicate similar good prospects also for ESA's MPAc laser retroreflector (MoonLIGHT with Pointing Actuators) to be launched in early 2027; pave the way for a new era of LLR observations and enhanced tests of GR, alternative gravity theories in general and improved lunar geophysics and geodesy.

title: The Population of Radio Hypernebulae from Mass-Transferring Massive Binaries
summary: Massive binary evolution is punctuated by brief phases of highly super-Eddington mass transfer (MT) onto neutron stars and black holes, presaging luminous transients such as supernovae, common envelope events, and gravitational wave sources. These hyper-accreting phases power relativistic jets and slower mass-loaded outflows, inflating extended nebulae of relativistic particles. Though observed in the local universe as ultra-luminous X-ray binaries and micro-quasars, the present census is biased against shorter-lived and hence rarer but potentially even more extreme MT systems: so-called ``hypernebulae'' (HNbe). We use the binary population synthesis code (\textsc{COMPAS}) to estimate the MT population, which spans a wide range of MT rates $\dot{M} \sim 10^{2-7}\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$ and source lifetimes $t_{\rm acc} \sim 10^{0-6}$ years. Combining this synthetic population with a semi-analytic model for their time-dependent radio emission, we predict the observable properties of HNbe over cosmic time. HNbe exhibit a broad GHz luminosity range extending to $L_{ν, \rm peak} \sim 10^{28-30}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$, and up to $\sim 10^{2}$ ($\sim 10^{5}$) HNbe are detectable by the wide-field radio surveys VLASS (DSA-2000) in our conservative model. A fraction of these systems should possess angular sizes and spatial offsets from star-forming regions (due to the first supernova kick) resolvable by VLBI. The most luminous donors, helium Hertzsprung-gap stars, may be detectable coincident with radio HNbe with Roman imaging out to distances $\sim 30$\,Mpc. Our findings suggest HNbe as promising probes of the pathways linking massive binaries to energetic transients.

authors: The Broad-Band X-ray Science Analysis Group
title: The Science and Technology of Broad-Band X-ray Astrophysics
comment: BBX-SAG Co-Chairs: Chien-Ting Chen (MSFC), Kristin K. Madsen (GSFC) & Daniel Stern (JPL). A report to the NASA Astrophysics Leadership and the Physics of the Cosmos Program office by the Broad-band X-ray Science Analysis Group https://science.nasa.gov/astrophysics/programs/physics-of-the-cosmos/community/bbx-sag/
summary:
Much of our understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena over the past decade has relied on coordinated observations extending from soft X-rays (<10 keV) to hard X-rays (>10 keV). While soft X-ray facilities remain abundant, focusing capabilities above ~10 keV are scarce, representing the primary gap for broad-band X-ray science. Simultaneous wide-band observations are essential to study thermal and non-thermal processes in extreme environments such as accretion discs, jets, and coronae. However, current high-energy observations remain limited by a lack of high angular resolution and sensitivity beyond Chandra's bandpass. With upcoming multi-messenger facilities set to dramatically increase variable and transient sources, a high angular resolution broad-band X-ray mission is critically needed.
  This report reviews the current landscape of high-energy facilities, outlines key science drivers, focusing on extragalactic accretion (the cosmic X-ray background) and Galactic compact objects, and examines the underlying technology landscape, including optics and detectors. Broad-band X-ray astrophysics is primed to address key questions from the Astro2020 Decadal Survey. While past focusing efforts have been limited to the Small Explorer class, technological advances now enable low-risk Probe- or Flagship-class architectures capable of delivering order-of-magnitude improvements in capabilities.

title: The Geometric Imprint of a Tilted Accretion Disk in Gravitational Waves
summary: Gravitational wave astronomy has opened a new window onto black holes and the dynamics of strong-field gravity, while accretion flows offer a complementary and natural laboratory for probing strong-field physics. In this work, we show that the gravitational wave emission from an initially tilted accretion disk carries a distinct imprint of its orientation. We perform three dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations and evaluate the gravitational waves through Teukolsky equation. For an aligned disk, the emission is concentrated in low-$|m|$ modes, where $m$ is the azimuthal quantum number. For the initially tilted disk, higher-$|m|$ modes make a larger relative contribution. As the tilted flow subsequently aligns with the black hole spin, the contribution of $|m|\ge2$ modes decreases, showing strong correlation with the tilt angle. This indicates that the gravitational waves generated by the black hole environment carries geometric information about the surrounding matter. Our results establish a route towards using multimode gravitational radiation to probe the geometry and dynamical evolution of accretion flows in the strong-field region.

title: A higher-order smoothness indicator as refinement criterion for Newtonian and relativistic MHD simulations
summary: Adaptive mesh refinement is a widely adopted strategy for grid-based numerical simulation codes to mitigate the high computational cost of multi-length scale problems. A robust and reliable mesh refinement criterion with minimal requirement for problem-specific tuning is critical for efficient and accurate simulations. Motivated by the oscillation indicators used in the spectral methods literature, we develop a new mesh refinement criterion employing a 5-point stencil for multi-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations, essentially extending the conventional 3-point Löhner scheme. We implement the criterion in the astrophysical fluid dynamics code AthenaK and test it across a variety of benchmark problems in Newtonian, special relativistic, and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, demonstrating its robustness and versatility.

title: Constraining Accretion Heating in Neutron Stars with Carbon Instability and Quiescent Cooling
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: In accreting neutron stars, different heating depths can produce similar quiescent cooling when the heating strength and core temperature are adjusted. For KS 1731-260, we compare thermal histories with accretion heating either in a shallower region that overlaps the carbon fuel layer or in a deeper region below it. Without the carbon instability condition, the two histories fit ten quiescent Chandra spectra nearly equally well. When local carbon instability is required at the observed superburst epoch, the deeper region needs stronger accretion heating than the shallower region. After the thermal and spectral parameters are refitted, the deeper history retains more heat beneath the fuel and produces excess early quiescent emission. A larger fitted absorbing column partly attenuates this excess but makes the late spectra too faint. The fuel temperatures at the superburst epoch are similar in the two histories, so the same prescribed energy release produces nearly identical superburst decays. Including carbon burial, consumption and nuclear heating reduces the accretion heating needed for rapid burning to begin near the observed superburst; shallower heating still fits the quiescent spectra better. This preference persists across the tested fuel depths, fusion rates, distances and absorption treatments. In synthetic examples, carbon in older material allows deeper heating to match the cooling of a shallower-heating reference. Inferring the heating location therefore requires a fuel distribution and thermal history consistent with ignition, burst emission and quiescent cooling.

title: Redrock: Spectroscopic Classification and Redshift Fitting for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument
summary: Redrock is a software package for spectroscopic classification and redshift fitting, designed to use the full information from spectroperfectionism outputs: flux-calibrated spectra, uncorrelated errors, and a per-spectrum resolution matrix encoding the non-Gaussian wavelength-dependent spectral line-spread function. Redrock was originally developed for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), but the Extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS) also used Redrock as their primary galaxy redshift fitter prior to DESI. This paper presents the algorithmic details of Redrock and its performance on DESI data. On spectra from DESI DR2, Redrock achieves a redshift recovery rate of approximately 98% for the Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) and Luminous Red Galaxies (LRG), 95.9% for Emission Line Galaxies (ELG), and 92.6% for quasars (QSO), and it delivers unbiased stellar radial velocities with a precision of roughly 5 km/s.

title: Positron escape from dark matter spikes in black hole X-ray binaries
summary: Chan and Lee present a model where the AMS-02 positron excess is explained by dark matter (DM) annihilation in spike halos around nearby black holes A0620-00 and XTE J1118+480. Their model assumes a uniform magnetic and diffusive environment en route to Earth. Thus, it depends on the assumption that one can ignore the small-scale, near-horizon environment in the diffusion-loss equation. We demonstrate that this is not the case. An accurate magnetic field model near the horizon means, without increasing the required cross-section by a factor of roughly 500 to 1400, depending on the transport near the horizon, the positron flux from these sources cannot account for a significant fraction of the AMS-02 excess.

title: Computation of complex dust grain optical properties: Optimisation method by equivalent representation (OMER)
summary: Computing the optical properties of dust grains is important for understanding various astrophysical environments. However, the numerical methods used to compute these properties require significant computing resources for irregularly shaped or inhomogeneous particles that are representative of realistic grown dust. This study aims to provide an efficient yet accurate Discrete dipole approximation (DDA) computation method for large aggregates with 'complex' monomers and structural details or compositional inhomogeneities. We propose the optimisation method by equivalent representation (OMER) method, which uses optimisation of the optical properties of a known monomer to find an equivalent homogeneous sphere. This sphere can then be used as a substitute for the complex monomer in large aggregates. The method provides a good approximation of complex monomers, as demonstrated in test cases involving large aggregates. Compared to existing methods, OMER shows greater accuracy, particularly in the range from visible to submillimetre wavelengths. The gain in computing time depends on the grain but can exceed two orders of magnitude. The proposed method provides a fast and accurate approximation for estimating the optical properties of materials with complex shapes and paves the way for efficient computation cross-sections for complex dust grain aggregates with thin core-mantle structures or hierarchical aggregates of large sizes.

title: Two Faint Tidal Disruption Events Discovered in a Pilot Search with the Wide Field Survey Telescope
summary: We report the discovery of TDE 2025alrm/WFST250129blnve and TDE 2025amkg/WFST251021dbmwk in the first six months of the wide-field survey (WFS) performed by the 2.5-meter Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST). Both events are apparently faint among known optical tidal disruption events (TDEs), with peak magnitudes of $g \sim 20.0$ and $g \sim 19.6$, respectively. Blackbody fits to the multi-band photometry yield roughly constant temperatures of $\sim 10^{4}$ K for both sources, with peak bolometric luminosities of $10^{43.6}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and $10^{43.8}$ erg s$^{-1}$, respectively. Optical spectra obtained during the declining phase display characteristic broad Balmer, He II, and N III emission lines, classifying both sources as H+He TDEs. Host-galaxy SED fitting suggests stellar masses on the order of $10^{9} M_{\odot}$ and black hole masses of $\sim10^{6} M_{\odot}$, which are typical of optically selected TDE hosts. The pilot discovery of these two faint TDEs along with dozens of candidates, demonstrates the capability of WFST to discover TDEs, owing to its exceptional survey depth. Furthermore, these events highlight the value of the $u$ band in multi-band surveys for TDE selection, particularly for distinguishing TDEs from supernovae at early phases. With continued operations, WFST is expected to substantially expand the known TDE population, especially by uncovering nearby low-luminosity events and high-redshift TDEs, both of which remain poorly explored.

title: A Butterfly Collector's View of Fast Radio Bursts: Repeating Sources Go Quiet within a Few Years
summary: How long repeating fast radio burst (FRB) sources stay active is key to their origins but poorly known as a population. We test this with unseen species estimation, a method first used to predict how many new butterfly species a further collecting trip would find. If each source keeps the same mean rate over time, the number of sources seen $k+1$ times in one window predicts how many bursts the sources seen $k$ times will emit in a later window. It assumes neither the burst rate distribution nor source distances. For the five years of CHIME/FRB Catalog 2, we measure the ratio $R$ of observed to predicted bursts against the gap $Δ$ between windows. A steady mean rate gives $R = 1$ at every $Δ$, so a change of $R$ with $Δ$ means that the sources change. $R$ is close to unity for $Δ\lesssim 60$ days and drops by half within one year. Neither steady nor randomly fluctuating sources reproduce this decline, unless the latter are mostly silent. Three models explain the data equally well: a lifetime of about three years, on/off activity with two-year active phases, or a mix of short- and long-lived sources. Fitted to the first three years alone, they correctly predict the further decline of $R$ in the last two years. Longer monitoring of $R$, and of whether silent sources come back to life, will distinguish them. Unlike butterfly species, FRB sources do not wait for the next collecting trip, so follow-up should start soon.

title: WFST0533buha (Bi'an): A Fast Blue Ultraluminous Transient Candidate with Unusual Blue/NUV Colors
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Revised manuscript submitted to AAS Journals
summary: We present WFST0533buha (Bi'an), a fast blue ultraluminous transient (FBUT) candidate discovered by the Wide Field Survey Telescope Deep High-cadence $ugr$-band Survey. The source brightened by approximately 2.5 mag in $u$ within 3 days and has a half-maximum timescale ($t_{1/2}$) shorter than 6 days. Two spectra show a blue, featureless continuum but do not provide a secure redshift. Einstein Probe observations yield only X-ray upper limits, while a faint radio counterpart was detected at 15 GHz with the VLA. The early $u$-band detection and intensive multiband coverage of Bi'an demonstrate the value of deep, high-cadence blue-band observations for discovering and characterizing FBUTs at early phases. Notably, Bi'an shows redder blue/NUV colors than AT 2018cow and AT 2024wpp, suggesting possible diversity in the short-wavelength properties of FBUTs.

title: Calibration of LHAASO-WCDA Energy Scale using Cosmic Ray Moon Shadow
comment: 13 pages, 13 Figures and 4 Tables are included in draft
summary: Cosmic-ray particles in the TeV range, originating outside the solar system, are partially blocked on their way to Earth by the Moon, producing a deficit in their flux known as the Moon shadow. This work presents a precision measurement of the westward shift of the Moon's shadow using 3.4 years of data from LHAASO's Water Cherenkov Detector Array (WCDA). We use this direct physical measurement, combined with four cosmic-ray composition models, each divided into five mass groups, to calibrate the detector's absolute energy response in the range of 4 - 37 TeV. We quantify the fractional deviation between the calibrated and simulated energy scales by determining a best-fit scale shift parameter of $ε$ =-0.04 $\pm$ 0.03. This yields a 95% confidence interval of -9% to +0.2% for the systematic energy scale deviation. Complementing the simulation based on hadronic interaction model, this geomagnetic calibration provides a data-driven physical validation of the simulated WCDA energy response, effectively bounding systematic uncertainties and refining the overall energy scale.

title: SN 2025wiu: A Slowly Evolving Type Ib Supernova with an Extraordinary Post-maximum Bump
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Revised manuscript submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Stripped-envelope supernovae (SESNe) originate from massive progenitors that have lost most or all of their outer envelopes prior to core collapse. Recent advances in optical time-domain surveys have revealed a growing population of peculiar SESNe with unusual light-curve morphologies, pointing to energy sources beyond the standard radioactive-decay scenario. In this work, we present multi-band photometric and spectroscopic observations of SN 2025wiu, a peculiar Type Ib supernova discovered by the Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST). SN 2025wiu is characterized by a high luminosity and exceptionally slow photometric evolution, with a prominent post-maximum bump peaking at $\sim50$ days after the primary maximum. Its early light curve also shows a weak excess consistent with shock-cooling emission from a compact progenitor with a radius of $\sim4\,R_\odot$. The spectra show only modest evolution, with persistently weak line features and no narrow emission lines detected even at $\sim110$ days after maximum. By modeling the primary peak and late-time tail with a combination of radioactive decay and additional energy sources, we isolate the post-maximum bump, which has a roughly symmetric profile with a peak luminosity of $\sim2.4 \times 10^{42}~\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ and a characteristic duration of $\sim42$ days. We discuss circumstellar medium (CSM) interaction, accretion, magnetar activity, and a double $^{56}$Ni distribution as possible origins of the bump. The latter three scenarios face challenges in reproducing the post-maximum bump, while delayed CSM interaction remains a possible explanation.

title: Possible origins of the two γ-ray components C0 and C1 in IC 443
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: Recent LHAASO observations of IC~443 reveal that its high-energy $γ$-ray emission can be decomposed into two components with clearly distinct spatial morphologies and spectral properties, namely the compact component C0 and component C1 with an angular extent of 0.67$^\circ$. We aim to explain the $γ$-ray emission mechanisms responsible for the two components in IC~443 and to further investigate their respective possible astrophysical counterparts. We model components C0 and C1 independently using two different physical scenarios. For component C0, we adopt an SNR-MC hadronic model that accounts for finite source-size effects to describe the escape and diffusion of high-energy particles and their $γ$-ray production via pp interactions with the surrounding molecular clouds. For component C1 , we employ a spatially dependent multi-zone leptonic transport model and describe the evolution of high-energy electrons under the combined action of advection, diffusion, and energy losses using a Fokker--Planck-type equation. The model reproduces the SEDs of components C0 and C1 well. Component C0 exhibits a pronounced $π^0$-decay feature, and the maximum energy of its escaping particles reaches the PeV scale. The $γ$-ray emission from component C1 can be explained by inverse Compton scattering. Its diffusion coefficient is approximately two orders of magnitude lower than that in the surrounding interstellar medium, and no significant synchrotron counterpart is detected. The $γ$-ray emission from IC~443 involves the combined action of multiple physical mechanisms. Component C0 may be a potential PeVatron candidate, whereas component C1 may correspond to a potential TeV halo candidate.

title: A lepto-hadronic perspective on the properties of the candidate neutrino-emitter blazar 5BZQ J0808+4950
summary: The role of active galactic nuclei in the production of high-energy neutrinos has been highlighted by the association of the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 with IceCube neutrino events. In particular, blazars, with their powerful jets, are potential sites of neutrino production via (photo-)hadronic interactions. The gamma-ray bright blazar 5BZQJ0808+4950 is consistent with a spatial anisotropy in the IceCube neutrino all-sky maps. An individual high-energy neutrino event, IC110929A, was also reported in the direction of this blazar. Although the correlation between the gamma-ray bright blazars and the neutrino production remains inconclusive, 5BZQ J0808+4950, with a luminous accretion disk serving as a photon field for the photo-hadronic interactions, offers the opportunity to test the relation between neutrino production and the radiative output of the blazar jet. We compile available multi-wavelength data and analyze the gamma-ray light curve of 5BZQ J0808+4950, leading us to define six contemporaneous epochs to model the source's spectral energy distribution and its evolution over time. We use a lepto-hadronic, time-dependent framework to model 5BZQ J0808+4950, taking into account external photon fields. We find that the solutions corresponding to the different states the source exhibits are explained mostly by a change in the particles' injection properties. The correlation between the predicted X-ray and the neutrino luminosity in this source is stronger than the correlation between gamma-ray and neutrino luminosity. We predict that the rate of neutrinos detectable by IceCube for this blazar ranges from $\sim 10^{-3}$ to $\sim10^{-1}$ neutrinos per epoch. Assuming Poisson statistics, the predicted neutrino number contemporaneous with the interval in which the high-energy neutrino event IC110929A was detected, is compatible with the detection of one neutrino.

title: Early spectra of AT2017gfo from scaled 3D merger ejecta: mass--velocity distribution, 3D structure, and treatment of line opacity
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present ARTIS radiative transfer calculations for neutron star merger ejecta with line-by-line opacities, wavelength-calibrated lanthanide data, and time-dependent r-process compositions and thermalisation, testing how the early kilonova depends on the mass-velocity distribution, dimensionality, and line treatment. We rescale 3D dynamical ejecta from a merger simulation in density and velocity to approximate AT2017gfo. Mass scaling alone provides good agreement with the bolometric light curve but inconsistent spectra. With velocities additionally halved, the model also reproduces the observed spectra at 1.4, 2.4, and (albeit less accurately) 3.4 days. The Sr II triplet contributes most to the 10500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ peak, and La III and Gd III to the 13500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ shoulder. Although hydrodynamically not fully self-consistent, this model is to our knowledge the first kilonova model based on calibrated atomic data that reproduces the light curve and main spectral features of the early AT2017gfo, suggesting that total (dynamical plus post-merger) ejecta with higher mass, lower velocity, and similar composition compared to our dynamical ejecta could explain AT2017gfo. A 2D azimuthal average mixes lanthanide-poor with lanthanide-rich regions, smooths the density, and makes the averaged model three times fainter at 1 day and redder throughout than the 3D model, highlighting the importance of 3D modelling. We compare the line-by-line macroatom treatment with expansion-opacity and line-binned schemes with thermal redistribution, using identical atomic data. Luminosities agree to $\lesssim 10$ per cent after 1 day, but the expansion-opacity scheme, unlike converged line-binned schemes, overestimates the spectral flux by up to 20 per cent, which can bias inferred abundances.

title: Investigating the Impact of SAX J1808.4-3658's Very Bright Thermonuclear X-ray Burst on the Accretion Disc with NICER
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We analyse a bright thermonuclear X-ray burst from the accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar (AMXP) SAX J1808.4-3658, the brightest burst detected by \textit{NICER} to date, to explore interactions between thermonuclear burst radiation and the accretion disc. This burst features a remarkable soft (<1.5 keV) excess in its spectra. For the first time, we simultaneously detect a reflection signal and the signature of an evolving persistent component, with our fits producing a peak persistent scaling factor $f_{a,1} = 59.6\pm0.6$. We find a high peak reflection fraction ($f_{r,1} = 0.82\pm0.15$) and a peak bolometric burst blackbody flux below Eddington (0.68$L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$) despite signatures of photospheric radius expansion. We detect a raised $N_\mathrm{H}$ ($\approx$34% above persistent emission) and raised disc blackbody temperature ($\approx$15% above persistent emission) during the burst's tail. This is the first time that spectroscopic evidence consistent with burst-induced disc heating has been found. We interpret that disc heating could cause the disc to puff up and inhibit burst photons, explaining the high reflection fraction and below-Eddington burst luminosity during the burst peak. We find an increasing count rate starting from $\approx$150s before the burst onset. Spectral analysis revealed a thermal component that evolves towards hotter temperatures closer to the onset of the burst. This is the second detection of this phenomenon from an AMXP. Lastly, we find that both the double-peaked structure and the "pause" in the rise are energy-dependent.

title: Rapid Equation of State Inference from Multiprobe Datasets
summary: Fully constraining the neutron star equation of state (EoS) requires combining observations from various channels that probe different density regimes. We perform a joint multimessenger inference of the equation of state using gravitational-wave observations from binary neutron star mergers, NICER mass-radius measurements of X-ray pulsars, and radio timing measurements of massive pulsars. We constrain the parametrized equation of state and perform Bayesian model selection among a set of candidate equations of state. The joint analysis produces a radius of $R_{1.4} = 11.93^{+1.02}_{-0.83} \, \rm km$ for a canonical $1.4 \, M_\odot$ neutron star, and a maximum non-rotating neutron star mass of $M_{\rm max} = 2.31^{+0.23}_{-0.23} \, M_\odot$ with $90\%$ credible intervals. Gravitational-wave and NICER observations constrain the equation of state at low to intermediate densities, while massive pulsar observations constrain it at high densities by requiring the equation of state to support the neutron star masses. We find no simple correlation between the stiffness of an EoS and Bayesian evidence because the observations probe the pressure at different density regimes. By combining constraints on the equation of state with Bayesian model selection using multimessenger data, our analysis connects macroscopic neutron star measurements to microscopic properties of candidate nuclear matter models.

authors: The Broad-Band X-ray Science Analysis Group
title: The Science and Technology of Broad-Band X-ray Astrophysics
comment: BBX-SAG Co-Chairs: Chien-Ting Chen (MSFC), Kristin K. Madsen (GSFC) & Daniel Stern (JPL). A report to the NASA Astrophysics Leadership and the Physics of the Cosmos Program office by the Broad-band X-ray Science Analysis Group https://science.nasa.gov/astrophysics/programs/physics-of-the-cosmos/community/bbx-sag/
summary:
Much of our understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena over the past decade has relied on coordinated observations extending from soft X-rays (<10 keV) to hard X-rays (>10 keV). While soft X-ray facilities remain abundant, focusing capabilities above ~10 keV are scarce, representing the primary gap for broad-band X-ray science. Simultaneous wide-band observations are essential to study thermal and non-thermal processes in extreme environments such as accretion discs, jets, and coronae. However, current high-energy observations remain limited by a lack of high angular resolution and sensitivity beyond Chandra's bandpass. With upcoming multi-messenger facilities set to dramatically increase variable and transient sources, a high angular resolution broad-band X-ray mission is critically needed.
  This report reviews the current landscape of high-energy facilities, outlines key science drivers, focusing on extragalactic accretion (the cosmic X-ray background) and Galactic compact objects, and examines the underlying technology landscape, including optics and detectors. Broad-band X-ray astrophysics is primed to address key questions from the Astro2020 Decadal Survey. While past focusing efforts have been limited to the Small Explorer class, technological advances now enable low-risk Probe- or Flagship-class architectures capable of delivering order-of-magnitude improvements in capabilities.

title: A higher-order smoothness indicator as refinement criterion for Newtonian and relativistic MHD simulations
summary: Adaptive mesh refinement is a widely adopted strategy for grid-based numerical simulation codes to mitigate the high computational cost of multi-length scale problems. A robust and reliable mesh refinement criterion with minimal requirement for problem-specific tuning is critical for efficient and accurate simulations. Motivated by the oscillation indicators used in the spectral methods literature, we develop a new mesh refinement criterion employing a 5-point stencil for multi-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations, essentially extending the conventional 3-point Löhner scheme. We implement the criterion in the astrophysical fluid dynamics code AthenaK and test it across a variety of benchmark problems in Newtonian, special relativistic, and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, demonstrating its robustness and versatility.
